rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jabir says the Companions practiced both forms of mut'a with the Prophet, until Umar forbade them and they stopped.
rows.anchor: فقال جابر فعلناهما مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم ثم نهانا عنهما عمر فلم نعد لهما

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A Muslim report has Umar say God had permitted His Messenger what He willed, command completion of Hajj and Umrah, and prohibit temporary marriage.
rows.anchor: فلما قام عمر قال إن الله كان يحل لرسوله ما شاء بما شاء فأتموا الحج والعمرة كما أمر الله وانتهوا عن نكاح هذه النساء

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: In the same report, Umar threatens stoning for any man who contracts a marriage for a fixed term.
rows.anchor: لا اوتى برجل نكح امرأة إلى أجل إلا رجمته

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: A sermon attributed to Umar says the two mut'as existed in the Prophet's time and that Umar now forbade and punished them.
rows.anchor: عن عمر أنه قال في خطبة متعتان كانتا على عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم وأنا أنهى عنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai says transmitters treated Umar's sermon as an established report.
rows.anchor: وخطبته هذه مما تسالم عليه أهل النقل وأرسلوه إرسال المسلمات

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: A report in al-Tabari attributes to Umar the prohibition and punishment of three practices: Hajj mut'a, women's mut'a, and the call hayya ala khayr al-amal.
rows.anchor: عن عمر أنه قال ثلاث كن على عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم أنا محرمهن ومعاقب عليهن متعة الحج

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: In Imran ibn Sawada's account, Umar says the Prophet permitted women's mut'a in a period of necessity; later abundance ended its use, though he states a man may marry for a handful and divorce after three.
rows.anchor: قال إن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم أحلها في زمان ضرورة ثم رجع الناس إلى السعة

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar's reported present-day alternative is a marriage for a handful followed by divorce after three.
rows.anchor: فالآن من شاء نكح بقبضة وفارق عن ثلاث بطلاق

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: In the same interview, Umar says he forbade an enslaved woman from being freed merely because she bore her master's child, and says he meant well and seeks forgiveness.
rows.anchor: قال ألحقت حرمة بحرمة وما أردت إلا الخير واستغفر الله

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: When challenged over harsh treatment of subjects, Umar describes himself as Muhammad's companion and says his governance combines restraint, feeding, warning, and limited physical force.
rows.anchor: أنا زميل محمد - وكان زامله في غزوة قرقرة الكدر - فوالله إني لأرتع فاشبع وأسقي فاروي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai says the reports conflict; their common result is that Caliph Umar prohibited mut'a on his own judgment, in connection with cases involving Amr ibn Hurayth and Rabi'a ibn Umayya.
rows.anchor: يرى ما فيها من التباين والتضارب ولا يتحصل للباحث في مضامينها غير أن عمر بن الخطاب أيام خلافته حرمها ونهى عنها لرأي رآه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Claims that scripture or Prophetic Sunnah abrogated mut'a do not yield a coherent conclusion; the reports contradict one another except that Umar imposed the ban and its penalty.
rows.anchor: أما حديث النسخ بالكتاب أو السنة فقد عرفت عدم رجوعه إلى محصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mut'a was practiced during the Prophet's lifetime with his approval or institution by Companions whom Al-Tabatabai says cannot be suspected of fornication, including Jabir, Ibn Masud, al-Zubayr, and Asma, mother of Ibn al-Zubayr.
rows.anchor: وأنها كانت سنة معمولا بها في زمن النبي في الجملة بتجويز منه صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A number of Companions and Successors held mut'a permissible, including Ibn Masud, Jabir, Amr ibn Hurayth, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.
rows.anchor: وأن في الصحابة والتابعين من كان يرى إباحتها كابن مسعود وجابر وعمرو بن حريث وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The severe disagreement over mut'a produced roughly fifteen different accounts of when and how it became forbidden.
rows.anchor: وذهابهم فيها إلى أقوال مختلفة عجيبة ربما أنهي إلى خمسة عشر قولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai distinguishes theological, legal, and exegetical questions; this book pursues whether 4:24 legislates mut'a and whether any Qur'anic verse or Prophetic report abrogated it.
rows.anchor: وهذا النحو الثالث من البحث هو الذي نعقبه في هذا الكتاب

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The critic says the verse concerns payment of the permanent-marriage dower, while Shi'a read it as a time-limited marriage for a day, week, or month, citing a non-canonical reading and transmitted reports.
rows.anchor: ذهبت الشيعة إلى أن المراد بالآية نكاح المتعة وهو نكاح المرأة إلى أجل معين كيوم أو أسبوع أو شهر مثلا

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The critic dismisses the reported reading as anomalous and not Qur'an, treating isolated additions as a Companion's interpretation rather than binding religious proof.
rows.anchor: فهي شاذة لم تثبت قرآنا وقد تقدم أن ما صحت فيه الرواية من مثل هذا آحادا فالزيادة فيه من قبيل التفسير

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The critic argues that a temporary-marriage man seeks sexual release rather than chastity, while a woman is hired successively by men, and supports the image with an unattributed poem.
rows.anchor: فإن كان هناك نوع ما من إحصان نفسه ومنعها من التنقل في زمن الزنا فإنه لا يكون فيه شيء ما من إحصان المرأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai replies that Shi'a do not treat anomalous readings as authoritative proof; they cite Companion readings as evidence of how those Companions understood the verse, alongside other Companion and Successor views.
rows.anchor: فكل مراجع يراجع كلامهم يرى أنهم لم يستدلوا بها استدلالهم بحجة معتبرة قاطعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports in which Companions transmit abrogation, like their readings, show that they understood the verse to indicate mut'a; citing them does not require Shi'a to affirm that abrogation actually occurred.
rows.anchor: كما لا يلزمهم القول بوقوع النسخ وإنما يستفيدون من الجميع من جهة الدلالة

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari says the Arabic root of nikah means intercourse; therefore defining sifah by ejaculation would also make nikah itself sifah and erase the distinction.
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري أصل النكاح في كلام العرب الوطء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If sexual desire and ejaculation make temporary marriage illicit, the same reasoning would make permanent marriage illicit when entered for sexual gratification.
rows.anchor: أن يكون النكاح الدائم بقصد قضاء الشهوة وصب الماء سفاحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Temporary marriage can protect against fornication and disrupted lineage, produce children, and establish a household, while easing marriage for people unable to afford permanence or prevented by travel and other circumstances.
rows.anchor: فإن جميع ما يترتب على النكاح الدائم من الفوائد كصون النفس عن الزنا والتوقي عن اختلال الأنساب وإيجاد النسل والولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The benefits and harms used to distinguish permanent marriage from mut'a can each occur in either form, so assigning chastity to one and vice to the other is plainly false.
rows.anchor: ودعوى أن النكاح الدائم بالطبع موضوع للفوائد السابقة ونكاح المتعة موضوع بالطبع لهذه المضار اللاحقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if mut'a is called sifah, sifah as the critic defines it is broader than zina and may include permanent marriage, especially when pursued for sexual gratification.
rows.anchor: بأن السفاح الذي فسره بصب الماء أعم من الزنا وربما شمل النكاح الدائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The critic gives no reason why a man may intend to preserve chastity through mut'a but a woman may not; the alleged difference is arbitrary.
rows.anchor: ما الفرق الفارق بين الرجل والمرأة في ذلك حتى يكون الرجل المتمتع يمكنه أن يحصن نفسه بنكاح المتعة من الزنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poem offers fantasy rather than evidence about religious law; Al-Tabatabai says it would be more apt beside Umar's report allowing a fixed-term marriage followed by three divorces.
rows.anchor: فماذا ينفع الشعر وهو نسيج خيالي الباطل أعرف عنده من الحق والغواية أمس به من الهداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because mut'a circulated openly among Muslims in the Prophet's presence, attacking it as illicit challenges its original legislation or approval by God and His Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقد كان دائرا بين المسلمين في أول الإسلام بمرئى من النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم ومسمع بلا شك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the Prophet first permitted mut'a from necessity, the verse is unrestricted and no verse or report validly abrogates it, so denying its continuing permissibility is an unsupported reinterpretation.
rows.anchor: مع إطلاقها وعدم صلاحية شيء من الآيات والروايات على نسخها فالقول بارتفاع إباحته تأول في دلالة الآية من غير دليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai asks why necessity would have been greater in the Prophet's era than under the early caliphs, when large armies campaigned across distant lands; poverty, warfare, and travel offered no clear distinction.
rows.anchor: هل كانت في زمن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم أشد وأعظم منها بعده ولا سيما في زمن الراشدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that present hardship is at least as severe: poverty, exploitative governments, widespread sexual temptation, and young workers or students unable to afford permanent marriage create the same alleged necessity.
rows.anchor: ولا يشك شاك ولن يشك في أن الضرورة الموقعة لهم في فحشاء الزنا واللواط وكل انخلاع شهواني عمدتها العجز من تهيئة نفقة البيت

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The critic invokes the guarded-private-parts passage to deny mut'a: its woman is not a wife, Shi'a omit ordinary spousal rights, permit many simultaneous partners, and do not treat the man as legally chaste.
rows.anchor: والمرأة المتمتع بها ليست زوجة فيكون لها على الرجل مثل الذي عليها بالمعروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai says the Meccan verses about guarding private parts do not contradict 4:24; if they banned mut'a, the Prophet's later permission would conflict with the Qur'an or require an impossible abrogation and revival.
rows.anchor: فهل كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم يبيح ما حرمه القرآن بإجازته المتعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Prophet's permission is certain and the cited Meccan verses are agreed to remain un-abrogated, the woman in mut'a must be a wife and the verses support its legality.
rows.anchor: وهذا في نفسه نعم الشاهد على أن المتمتع بها زوجة وأن المتعة نكاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the critic's own reading, calling mut'a forbidden under the Meccan verses would make the Prophet's permission abrogate them, which no Muslim accepts; that contradiction instead supports marriage status.
rows.anchor: ومن الضروري بحسب النقل أن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم رخص في المتعة ولولا كون المتمتع بها زوجة

rows.speaker: سليمان بن يسار
rows.claim: A report attributed to Umar says people should distinguish nikah from illicit sex; Al-Tabatabai reads this wording as acknowledging mut'a as a form of marriage.
rows.anchor: عن سليمان بن يسار " بينوا حتى يعرف النكاح من السفاح "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Companions and Successors, even Umar, called mut'a nikah; it was a wife under Qur'anic and early Muslim usage, while Umar's ban later left permanent marriage as the conventional meaning.
rows.anchor: كون المتعة نكاحا وكون المتمتع بها زوجة في عرف القرآن ولسان السلف من الصحابة ومن تلاهم من التابعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute over spousal rights turns on the meaning of wife: Shi'a apply the Qur'anic category to mut'a, but do not apply every status associated with the later juristic convention for permanent marriage.
rows.anchor: أما الزوجة في عرف القرآن فإنهم يعطونها أحكامها من غير استثناء وأما الزوجة في عرف المتشرعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the earlier discussion, Al-Tabatabai read ihsan in the verse as chastity rather than marriage, since the verse also covers enslaved women; even if it means marriage, mut'a is included.
rows.anchor: أن ظاهرها من جهة شمولها ملك اليمين أن المراد بالإحصان إحصان التعفف دون الازدواج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No Qur'anic rule requires stoning; Sunnah may specify mut'a from inheritance, maintenance, divorce, and waiting-period rules, as it specifies other broad legal verses.
rows.anchor: فإنما هو لبيان أو لتخصيص من السنة كسائر أحكام الزوجية من الميراث والنفقة والطلاق والعدد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic verses may state only a basic rule or express a generality; Sunnah can qualify them without contradiction, as in inheritance and divorce for apostates, annulment for defects, and maintenance during disobedience.
rows.anchor: فما يطرأ عليها من القيود بيانات من غير تخصيص ولا تقييد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The allegation that Shi'a impose no waiting period is false: their legal works require two menstrual periods, and reports from the Imams support this.
rows.anchor: فهذه جوامع الشيعة وهذه كتبهم الفقهية مملوءة بأن عدة المتمتع بها حيضتان

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The critic synthesizes reports as successive permissions and prohibitions ending in a permanent ban, initially allowing mut'a only to ease abstinence from zina during distant military campaigns.
rows.anchor: كان يرخص لأصحابه فيها في بعض الغزوات ثم نهاهم عنها ثم رخص فيها مرة أو مرتين ثم نهاهم عنها نهيا مؤبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai says that chronology does not fit the reports already cited; their contradictions disprove the critic's proposed reconciliation.
rows.anchor: ما ذكره أن مجموع الروايات تدل على الترخيص في بعض الغزوات ثم النهي ثم الترخيص فيها مرة أو مرتين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The critic presents mut'a as a pre-Islamic form of zina that the Prophet gradually prohibited, like wine, retaining it temporarily to ease acceptance of a complete ban; he says zina was more common among enslaved women.
rows.anchor: يرى أهل السنة أن الرخصة في المتعة مرة أو مرتين يقرب من التدريج في منع الزنا منعا باتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai calls that account a degrading game with sacred legislation: if Meccan verses already forbade mut'a, repeated Prophetic permissions would repeatedly abrogate and revive those verses.
rows.anchor: وهل هذا إلا نسبة اللعب بكتاب الله إليه صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai lists Meccan prohibitions of zina: 17:32, the comprehensive ban on indecencies in 6:151, 7:33, and 23:5–7; these contradict a gradual ban on mut'a.
rows.anchor: ولا تقربوا الزنا إنه كان فاحشة وساء سبيلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the critic says 23:5–7 forbids mut'a, his theory makes God prohibit it and the infallible Prophet later authorize it; authorization from God would mean God commands indecency.
rows.anchor: إن الله سبحانه حرمها تحريما باتا ثم النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai invokes 17:73–75: God says He protected the Prophet from nearly yielding to pressure to alter revelation and threatened doubled punishment if he did.
rows.anchor: وقد شدد الله تعالى على نبيه صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم في هذه الخلة بعينها قال تعالى
